claim: Diabetic foot ulcers are the leading cause of lower extremity amputations in the United States.
source: Diabetic foot ulcers are the leading cause of lower extremity amputations in the United States and are responsible for more hospitalizations than any other complication of diabetes (Sen et al., 2009; Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Reiber et al., 1999; Frykberg, 2002; Boulton, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Sen et al., 2009; Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Reiber et al., 1999; Frykberg, 2002; Boulton, 2000).

claim: Diabetic foot ulcers are responsible for more hospitalizations than any other complication of diabetes.
source: Diabetic foot ulcers are the leading cause of lower extremity amputations in the United States and are responsible for more hospitalizations than any other complication of diabetes (Sen et al., 2009; Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Reiber et al., 1999; Frykberg, 2002; Boulton, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Sen et al., 2009; Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Reiber et al., 1999; Frykberg, 2002; Boulton, 2000).

claim: Infection with pathogenic bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major co-morbidity that contributes to impaired healing in diabetic ulcers.
source: Infection with pathogenic bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, is a major co-morbidity that contributes to impaired healing in diabetic ulcers (Kirketerp-Møller et al., 2008; Gjødsbøl et al., 2006; Dowd et al., 2008; Redel et al., 2013; Goldufsky et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Kirketerp-Møller et al., 2008; Gjødsbøl et al., 2006; Dowd et al., 2008; Redel et al., 2013; Goldufsky et al., 2015).

claim: Neutrophils are the first inflammatory leukocytes that infiltrate into the wound.
source: Neutrophils are the first inflammatory leukocytes that infiltrate into the wound (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kim et al., 2008).

claim: Neutrophils have antimicrobial functions mediated by phagocytosis, bursts of reactive oxygen species (ROS), antimicrobial production, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET).
source: In addition to their antimicrobial functions mediated by phagocytosis, bursts of reactive oxygen species (ROS), antimicrobial (AMP) production, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) (Dovi et al., 2004; Brinkmann et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dovi et al., 2004; Brinkmann et al., 2004).

claim: Neutrophils express various cytokines and chemokines that set the stage for subsequent inflammatory and non-inflammatory responses.
source: they also express various cytokines and chemokines that set the stage for the subsequent inflammatory and non-inflammatory responses, which further contribute to infection control and partake in healing processes (Velnar et al., 2009; Fenteany et al., 2000; Schäfer and Werner, 2008; Martin, 1997; Diegelmann and Evans, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Velnar et al., 2009; Fenteany et al., 2000; Schäfer and Werner, 2008; Martin, 1997; Diegelmann and Evans, 2004).

claim: Diabetic ulcers suffer from persistent non-resolving inflammation characterized by increased neutrophils.
source: There appears to be a disconnect in that diabetic ulcers suffer from persistent non-resolving inflammation – characterized by increased neutrophils – yet they fail to control infection.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation in the manuscript text.

claim: Bactericidal functional impairments in diabetic neutrophils underlie defective infection control in diabetic wounds.
source: Bactericidal functional impairments in diabetic neutrophils (PMNs) is thought to underlie defective infection control in diabetic wound (Repine et al., 1980; Gallacher et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Repine et al., 1980; Gallacher et al., 1995).

claim: The impairment severity in diabetic neutrophils has been associated with the degree of hyperglycemia.
source: although the impairment severity has been associated with the degree of hyperglycemia (Repine et al., 1980)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Repine et al., 1980).

claim: Exposure to high-glucose levels may be a contributing factor to impairments in diabetic neutrophils.
source: although the impairment severity has been associated with the degree of hyperglycemia (Repine et al., 1980), suggesting that exposure to high-glucose levels may be a contributing factor to these impairments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the association between hyperglycemia and impairment severity.

claim: Diabetic neutrophils isolated from the blood of diabetic patients display impaired chemotactic response.
source: In addition to impaired bactericidal functions, diabetic neutrophils – (isolated from the blood of diabetic patients) – also display impaired chemotactic response (Delamaire et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Delamaire et al., 1997).

claim: Excessive neutrophil response is blamed as a major impediment to healing in chronic diabetic ulcers.
source: This peculiar functional impairment in diabetic neutrophils has not received much attention primarily because it appears to contradict the clinical findings which finds and blames excessive neutrophil response as a major impediment to healing in chronic diabetic ulcers (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008).

claim: db/db wounds contained 2–4 log orders more bacteria than normal wounds.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Goldufsky et al., 2015), db/db wounds contained 2–4 log orders more bacteria than normal wounds, indicating that diabetic wounds are vulnerable to increased infection with P. aeruginosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with a previous report (Goldufsky et al., 2015).

claim: Diabetic wounds are vulnerable to increased infection with P. aeruginosa.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Goldufsky et al., 2015), db/db wounds contained 2–4 log orders more bacteria than normal wounds, indicating that diabetic wounds are vulnerable to increased infection with P. aeruginosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that db/db wounds contained 2–4 log orders more bacteria than normal wounds, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diabetic mice exhibited substantially reduced neutrophil influx in wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3.
source: Surprisingly, diabetic mice exhibited substantially reduced neutrophil influx in wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3 but significantly higher neutrophil contents in day 6 and day 10, as compared to normal wounds (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1a–b.

claim: Diabetic mice exhibited significantly higher neutrophil contents in day 6 and day 10 wounds compared to normal wounds.
source: Surprisingly, diabetic mice exhibited substantially reduced neutrophil influx in wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3 but significantly higher neutrophil contents in day 6 and day 10, as compared to normal wounds (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1a–b.

claim: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) was substantially reduced in diabetic wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3.
source: Corroborating these data, myeloperoxidase (MPO) -– (a marker for primarily activated neutrophils Klebanoff, 2005) – was also substantially reduced in diabetic wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3 but significantly higher in day 10 wounds (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by MPO analysis data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) was significantly higher in day 10 diabetic wounds.
source: Corroborating these data, myeloperoxidase (MPO) -– (a marker for primarily activated neutrophils Klebanoff, 2005) – was also substantially reduced in diabetic wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3 but significantly higher in day 10 wounds (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by MPO analysis data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: MPO is a marker for primarily activated neutrophils.
source: Corroborating these data, myeloperoxidase (MPO) -– (a marker for primarily activated neutrophils Klebanoff, 2005) – was also substantially reduced in diabetic wounds early after injury at days 1 and 3 but significantly higher in day 10 wounds (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Klebanoff, 2005).

claim: Flow cytometry analysis corroborated the inadequate neutrophil trafficking into diabetic wounds early after injury.
source: Assessment of neutrophil contents in day one normal and diabetic infected wounds by flow cytometry – where neutrophils were identified as CD45+Ly6C/GhiCD11bhi (Kuijpers et al., 1991; Atzeni et al., 2002) – further corroborated the inadequate neutrophil trafficking into diabetic wounds early after injury (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neutrophils can be identified as CD45+Ly6C/GhiCD11bhi by flow cytometry.
source: Assessment of neutrophil contents in day one normal and diabetic infected wounds by flow cytometry – where neutrophils were identified as CD45+Ly6C/GhiCD11bhi (Kuijpers et al., 1991; Atzeni et al., 2002) – further corroborated the inadequate neutrophil trafficking into diabetic wounds early after injury (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kuijpers et al., 1991; Atzeni et al., 2002).

claim: Neutrophil response is delayed in diabetic wounds, rendering these wounds vulnerable to infection early after injury.
source: These data indicated that neutrophil response – (which is needed to combat infection) – is delayed in diabetic wounds, rendering these wounds vulnerable to infection early after injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing reduced neutrophil influx in diabetic wounds early after injury.

claim: The initial neutrophil chemotaxis in response to injury or infection involves the activation of G protein–coupled formyl peptide receptor (FPR) by N-formyl peptides.
source: However, the initial neutrophil chemotaxis in response to injury or infection involves the activation of G protein–coupled formyl peptide receptor (FPR) by N-formyl peptides, such as fMet-Leu-Phe (fMLF, a.k.a., fMLP), which is released either by injured tissues or by invading bacteria (de Oliveira et al., 2016; Roupé et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (de Oliveira et al., 2016; Roupé et al., 2010).

claim: FPR1 appears to be the primary FPR in responding to infection, as it has significantly higher affinity for bacterial formyl peptides.
source: FPR1 and FPR2 are two FPR implicated in these responses, although FPR1 appears to be the primary FPR in responding to infection, as it has significantly higher affinity for bacterial formyl peptides, whereas FPR2 has a broader range of ligands than FPR1 and has been implicated in the resolution of inflammation in response to pro-resolving agonists, such as Annexin A1 (Ye et al., 2009; Jeong and Bae, 2020; Bena et al., 2012; Yazid et al., 2012; Serhan and Savill, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ye et al., 2009; Jeong and Bae, 2020; Bena et al., 2012; Yazid et al., 2012; Serhan and Savill, 2005).

claim: FPR2 has a broader range of ligands than FPR1 and has been implicated in the resolution of inflammation in response to pro-resolving agonists, such as Annexin A1.
source: FPR1 and FPR2 are two FPR implicated in these responses, although FPR1 appears to be the primary FPR in responding to infection, as it has significantly higher affinity for bacterial formyl peptides, whereas FPR2 has a broader range of ligands than FPR1 and has been implicated in the resolution of inflammation in response to pro-resolving agonists, such as Annexin A1 (Ye et al., 2009; Jeong and Bae, 2020; Bena et al., 2012; Yazid et al., 2012; Serhan and Savill, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ye et al., 2009; Jeong and Bae, 2020; Bena et al., 2012; Yazid et al., 2012; Serhan and Savill, 2005).

claim: Activation of FPR leads to the upregulation and secretion of leukotriene B4 (LTB4), which activates BLT1.
source: Activation of FPR then leads to the upregulation and secretion of lipid signals, such as the leukotriene B4 (LTB4), which in turn activate BLT1, (another G-protein-coupled receptor on neutrophils), amplifying neutrophil trafficking by enhancing the signaling through FPR (Afonso et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Afonso et al., 2012).

claim: BLT1 activation in neutrophils by LTB4 results in upregulation and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β.
source: BLT1 activation in neutrophils by LTB4 also results in upregulation and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β which in turn induces the expression and secretion of other ligands (i.e. CCL3 and CXCL1) in tissue resident epithelial cells and inflammatory leukocytes, which further amplify neutrophil trafficking and other inflammatory leukocytes including monocytes, by engaging their respective auxiliary receptors, such as CCR1 and CXCR2 (36, 37, 44, 45).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (references 36, 37, 44, 45 in the manuscript).

claim: db/db neutrophils were significantly impaired in their ability to chemotax toward fMLF compared to normal neutrophils isolated from C57BL/6.
source: Compared to normal neutrophils isolated from C57BL/6, db/db neutrophils were significantly impaired in their ability to chemotax toward fMLF (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Expression of FPR1 was significantly diminished in db/db neutrophils.
source: Consistent with reduced signaling through the FPR in response to bacterial fMLF, expression of FPR1 was significantly diminished in db/db neutrophils, as assessed by western blotting (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 2b–c.

claim: The percentage of FPR1-positive neutrophils was significantly reduced in day one diabetic wounds.
source: Further corroborating these data, the percentage of FPR1-positive neutrophils was significantly reduced in day one diabetic wounds, after accounting for reduced number of neutrophils in diabetic wounds early after injury by assessing equal number of neutrophils by flow cytometry (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Various studies have shown direct correlations between plasma glucose levels and prevalence and/or severity of infection in diabetic patients.
source: Various studies have shown direct correlations between plasma glucose levels and prevalence and/or severity of infection in diabetic patients (Rayfield et al., 1982; Latham et al., 2001; Zerr et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rayfield et al., 1982; Latham et al., 2001; Zerr et al., 1997).

claim: Short-term and long-term glycemic control in diabetic rats significantly improved their ability to control Staphylococcus aureus infection.
source: Consistent with these reports, short-term and long-term glycemic control in diabetic rats, has been shown to significantly improve their ability to control Staphylococcus aureus infection (Kroin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kroin et al., 2015).

claim: 1 hr exposure to high glucose in diabetic range had no effect on viability of neutrophils.
source: Of note, 1 hr exposure to high glucose in diabetic range had no effect on viability of neutrophils.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation in the manuscript text.

claim: Exposure to high glucose levels caused significant reduction in chemotactic response to fMLF in both human and mouse neutrophils.
source: Exposure to high glucose levels caused significant reduction in chemotactic response to fMLF in both human and mouse neutrophils (Figure 2e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 2e–f.

claim: Neutrophils exposed to normal glucose showed a bell-shaped curve in their chemotaxis response toward fMLF concentrations (0.01–1000 nM) with 100 nM being the optimum concentration.
source: While neutrophils exposed to normal glucose showed a bell-shaped curve in their chemotaxis response toward fMLF concentrations (0.01–1000 nM) with 100 nM being the optimum concentration, neutrophils exposed to high glucose showed flat chemotaxis response toward these fMLF concentrations, trending toward lower chemotaxis at higher concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neutrophils exposed to high glucose showed flat chemotaxis response toward fMLF concentrations, trending toward lower chemotaxis at higher concentrations.
source: While neutrophils exposed to normal glucose showed a bell-shaped curve in their chemotaxis response toward fMLF concentrations (0.01–1000 nM) with 100 nM being the optimum concentration, neutrophils exposed to high glucose showed flat chemotaxis response toward these fMLF concentrations, trending toward lower chemotaxis at higher concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: High fMLF ligand concentrations cannot rescue chemotaxis signaling through FPR in neutrophils exposed to high glucose.
source: While neutrophils exposed to normal glucose showed a bell-shaped curve in their chemotaxis response toward fMLF concentrations (0.01–1000 nM) with 100 nM being the optimum concentration, neutrophils exposed to high glucose showed flat chemotaxis response toward these fMLF concentrations, trending toward lower chemotaxis at higher concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that high fMLF ligand concentrations cannot rescue chemotaxis signaling through FPR in neutrophils exposed to high glucose.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that neutrophils exposed to high glucose showed flat chemotaxis response toward fMLF concentrations.

claim: Exposure to high glucose caused significant reductions in FPR1 surface expression.
source: Of note, exposure to high glucose also caused significant reductions in FPR1 surface expression, FPR1 and PLCγ protein levels, as well as cAMP levels (Figure 2g–k)
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2g–k.

claim: Exposure to high glucose caused significant reductions in FPR1 and PLCγ protein levels.
source: Of note, exposure to high glucose also caused significant reductions in FPR1 surface expression, FPR1 and PLCγ protein levels, as well as cAMP levels (Figure 2g–k)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 2g–k.

claim: Exposure to high glucose caused significant reductions in cAMP levels.
source: Of note, exposure to high glucose also caused significant reductions in FPR1 surface expression, FPR1 and PLCγ protein levels, as well as cAMP levels (Figure 2g–k)
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2g–k.

claim: FPR1, PLCγ, and cAMP are all required to mediate FPR-mediated chemotaxis in neutrophils.
source: Of note, exposure to high glucose also caused significant reductions in FPR1 surface expression, FPR1 and PLCγ protein levels, as well as cAMP levels (Figure 2g–k), which are all required to mediate FPR-mediated chemotaxis in neutrophils (Afonso et al., 2012; Heit et al., 2002; Hirsch et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Afonso et al., 2012; Heit et al., 2002; Hirsch et al., 2000).

claim: 1 hr exposure to high glucose resulted in significant reductions in the FPR1 and PLCγ transcription.
source: Corroborating these data, 1 hr exposure to high glucose resulted in significant reductions in the FPR1 and PLCγtranscription as determined by mRNA analysis by RT-PCR (Figure 2l–m).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2l–m.

claim: Exposure to high glucose significantly reduced the expression of FPR1 both at the transcriptional and translational levels at all timepoints (1, 2, or 3 hr post exposure).
source: Data indicated that exposure to high glucose significantly reduced the expression of FPR1 both at the transcriptional and translational levels at all timepoints, indicating that exposure to high glucose dampens the expression of FPR1 in a sustained manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to high glucose dampens the expression of FPR1 in a sustained manner.
source: Data indicated that exposure to high glucose significantly reduced the expression of FPR1 both at the transcriptional and translational levels at all timepoints, indicating that exposure to high glucose dampens the expression of FPR1 in a sustained manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that exposure to high glucose significantly reduced the expression of FPR1 at all timepoints.

claim: High glucose similarly dampened the expression of FPR2 both at transcriptional and translational levels.
source: Of note, high glucose similarly dampened the expression of FPR2 both at transcriptional and translational levels, indicating that the adverse impact of high glucose is not restricted to FPR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The adverse impact of high glucose is not restricted to FPR1.
source: Of note, high glucose similarly dampened the expression of FPR2 both at transcriptional and translational levels, indicating that the adverse impact of high glucose is not restricted to FPR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that high glucose dampened the expression of both FPR1 and FPR2.

claim: Elevated glucose levels in diabetes is responsible for the reduced chemotactic response through FPR in diabetic neutrophils.
source: Collectively, these data indicated that elevated glucose levels in diabetes is responsible for the reduced chemotactic response through FPR in diabetic neutrophils.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that exposure to high glucose reduces chemotactic response through FPR.

claim: None of the chemotaxis receptors appear to be essential on their own and their defects can be overcome by engaging other receptors.
source: Although, the initial neutrophil chemotactic response through FPR and the amplification of neutrophil chemotactic responses via other auxiliary receptors are interconnected and occur sequentially in vivo (Liu et al., 2012; Sadik et al., 2011; Futosi et al., 2013; Ng et al., 2011; Afonso et al., 2012; Chou et al., 2010), none of these receptors appear to be essential on their own and their defects can be overcome by engaging other receptors (Chou et al., 2010; Lämmermann et al., 2013; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chou et al., 2010; Lämmermann et al., 2013; Park et al., 2009).

claim: Chronic diabetic ulcers suffer from increased neutrophil contents.
source: Chronic diabetic ulcers suffer from increased neutrophil contents (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008), indicating that diabetic neutrophils are capable of migrating into the wound, albeit at dysregulated kinetics as our data show (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008).

claim: Diabetic neutrophils are capable of migrating into the wound, albeit at dysregulated kinetics.
source: Chronic diabetic ulcers suffer from increased neutrophil contents (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008), indicating that diabetic neutrophils are capable of migrating into the wound, albeit at dysregulated kinetics as our data show (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that chronic diabetic ulcers have increased neutrophil contents and the data in Figure 1 showing delayed neutrophil trafficking.

claim: CCL3 engages multiple auxiliary receptors, namely CCR1, CCR4, and CCR5.
source: The reason we focused on CCL3 was because it engages multiple auxiliary receptors, namely CCR1, CCR4, and CCR5 (Ramos et al., 2005; da Silva et al., 2017; Yoshie and Matsushima, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ramos et al., 2005; da Silva et al., 2017; Yoshie and Matsushima, 2015).

claim: CCR1 is an important receptor that is implicated in neutrophil trafficking to post-ischemic tissues.
source: Of note, CCR1 is an important receptor that is implicated in neutrophil trafficking to post-ischemic tissues (Reichel et al., 2006) and ischemia is an important co-morbidity associated with impaired healing in diabetic wound (Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Armstrong et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Reichel et al., 2006).

claim: Ischemia is an important co-morbidity associated with impaired healing in diabetic wound.
source: Of note, CCR1 is an important receptor that is implicated in neutrophil trafficking to post-ischemic tissues (Reichel et al., 2006) and ischemia is an important co-morbidity associated with impaired healing in diabetic wound (Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Armstrong et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brem and Tomic-Canic, 2007; Armstrong et al., 1998).

claim: Exposure to glucose in the diabetic range did not affect the chemotactic responses toward CCL3 in human or mouse neutrophils.
source: Data indicated that exposure to glucose in the diabetic range did not affect the chemotactic responses toward CCL3 in human or mouse neutrophils (Figure 3a–b)
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 3a–b.

claim: CCR1 expression remained unaffected in neutrophils after exposure to high glucose for 1 hr as assessed by Western blotting.
source: In line with chemotaxis data, CCR1 expression remained unaffected in neutrophils after exposure to high glucose for 1 hr as assessed by Western blotting (Figure 3c–d)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3c–d.

claim: CCR1 expression remained unaffected in neutrophils after exposure to high glucose for 1 hr as assessed by mRNA analysis.
source: In line with chemotaxis data, CCR1 expression remained unaffected in neutrophils after exposure to high glucose for 1 hr as assessed by Western blotting (Figure 3c–d), by mRNA analysis (Figure 3e)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: CCR1 surface expression remained unaffected in neutrophils after exposure to high glucose for 1 hr.
source: In line with chemotaxis data, CCR1 expression remained unaffected in neutrophils after exposure to high glucose for 1 hr as assessed by Western blotting (Figure 3c–d), by mRNA analysis (Figure 3e), and by surface expression analysis (Figure 3f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3f–g.

claim: CCR1 expression was similar in neutrophils isolated from the blood of db/db and C57BL/6 mice.
source: Further corroborating these data, CCR1 expression was similar in neutrophils isolated from the blood of db/db and C57BL/6 mice (Figure 3h–i)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3h–i.

claim: The percentage of CCR1-positive neutrophils in db/db day 1 wounds were similar to C57BL/6 day 1 wounds.
source: and the percentage of CCR1-positive neutrophils in db/db day 1 wounds were similar to C57BL/6 day 1 wounds, after accounting for the reduced number of leukocytes in day one diabetic wounds by assessing equal number of neutrophils by flow cytometry (Figure 3j).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Surface expression of auxiliary receptor CXCR2 on neutrophils was unaffected by high glucose exposure.
source: Of note, surface expression of auxiliary receptor CXCR2, (another important auxiliary receptor involved in the amplification of neutrophil response in wound and toward infection [de Oliveira et al., 2016; Brubaker et al., 2013]), on neutrophils and chemotaxis through the CXCR2 in response to CXCL1 (a.k.a. KC) – a known ligand for CXCR2 (Chintakuntlawar and Chodosh, 2009) – were also unaffected by high glucose exposure in neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: Chemotaxis through the CXCR2 in response to CXCL1 was unaffected by high glucose exposure in neutrophils.
source: Of note, surface expression of auxiliary receptor CXCR2, (another important auxiliary receptor involved in the amplification of neutrophil response in wound and toward infection [de Oliveira et al., 2016; Brubaker et al., 2013]), on neutrophils and chemotaxis through the CXCR2 in response to CXCL1 (a.k.a. KC) – a known ligand for CXCR2 (Chintakuntlawar and Chodosh, 2009) – were also unaffected by high glucose exposure in neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: CXCR2 is an important auxiliary receptor involved in the amplification of neutrophil response in wound and toward infection.
source: Of note, surface expression of auxiliary receptor CXCR2, (another important auxiliary receptor involved in the amplification of neutrophil response in wound and toward infection [de Oliveira et al., 2016; Brubaker et al., 2013]), on neutrophils and chemotaxis through the CXCR2 in response to CXCL1 (a.k.a. KC) – a known ligand for CXCR2 (Chintakuntlawar and Chodosh, 2009) – were also unaffected by high glucose exposure in neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (de Oliveira et al., 2016; Brubaker et al., 2013).

claim: CXCL1 is a known ligand for CXCR2.
source: Of note, surface expression of auxiliary receptor CXCR2, (another important auxiliary receptor involved in the amplification of neutrophil response in wound and toward infection [de Oliveira et al., 2016; Brubaker et al., 2013]), on neutrophils and chemotaxis through the CXCR2 in response to CXCL1 (a.k.a. KC) – a known ligand for CXCR2 (Chintakuntlawar and Chodosh, 2009) – were also unaffected by high glucose exposure in neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chintakuntlawar and Chodosh, 2009).

claim: At least CCR1 and CXCR2 auxiliary receptors may remain functional under diabetic conditions.
source: Collectively, these data suggested that at least CCR1 and CXCR2 auxiliary receptors may remain functional under diabetic conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that CCR1 and CXCR2 expression and chemotaxis through these receptors are unaffected by high glucose.

claim: Production of ligands (including CCL3) for auxiliary receptors in tissue ultimately depends on FPR activation.
source: As discussed above, production of ligands (including CCL3) for auxiliary receptors in tissue ultimately depends on FPR activation (Afonso et al., 2012; Chou et al., 2010; Su and Richmond, 2015; Luster et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Afonso et al., 2012; Chou et al., 2010; Su and Richmond, 2015; Luster et al., 2005).

claim: Leukocytes (i.e. neutrophils) are major cellular sources of ligands for auxiliary receptors (including CCL3).
source: In addition, leukocytes (i.e. neutrophils) are major cellular sources of ligands for auxiliary receptors (including CCL3) (Ridiandries et al., 2018; Tecchio et al., 2014; Sanz and Kubes, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ridiandries et al., 2018; Tecchio et al., 2014; Sanz and Kubes, 2012).

claim: Increased expression of immunosuppressive IL-10 in diabetic wounds early after injury has been shown to lead to significant reduction in toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling in diabetic wounds early after injury.
source: Moreover, increased expression of immunosuppressive IL-10 in diabetic wounds early after injury has been shown to lead to significant reduction in toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling in diabetic wounds early after injury (Roy et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roy et al., 2021).

claim: TLR signaling has been implicated in the production of ligands (including CCL3) for auxiliary receptors.
source: And TLR signaling has been implicated in the production of ligands (including CCL3) for auxiliary receptors (Kochumon et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kochumon et al., 2020; Ahmad et al., 2019).

claim: CCL3 expression was substantially reduced in day one diabetic wounds.
source: In line with our hypothesis, CCL3 expression was substantially reduced in day one diabetic wounds, as assessed by mRNA analysis and Western blotting (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR and western blotting data shown in Figure 4a–c.

claim: One-time topical treatment with CCL3 significantly increased neutrophil trafficking in day one diabetic wounds.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, one-time topical treatment with CCL3 significantly increased neutrophil trafficking in day one diabetic wounds, as assessed by Ly6G histological analysis (Figure 4d–e), by flow cytometry (Figure 4f), and by MPO analysis (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis, flow cytometry, and MPO analysis data shown in Figure 4d–g.

claim: CCL3 treatment significantly enhanced the ability of diabetic wounds to control infection.
source: Importantly, CCL3 treatment significantly enhanced the ability of diabetic wounds to control infection, as demonstrated by nearly a two log-order reduction in the number of bacteria contained in the CCL3-treated db/db wounds (Figure 4h).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU count data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Anti-Ly6G reduced the neutrophil contents in circulation by ~97%.
source: Anti-Ly6G reduced the neutrophil contents in circulation by ~97% and in wound by ~75% (Figure 4i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Anti-Ly6G reduced the neutrophil contents in wound by ~75%.
source: Anti-Ly6G reduced the neutrophil contents in circulation by ~97% and in wound by ~75% (Figure 4i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by MPO analysis data shown in Figure 4i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Neutrophil-depletion resulted in ~2 log-order more bacteria in diabetic wounds.
source: Neutrophil-depletion also resulted in ~2 log-order more bacteria in diabetic wounds, indicating that despite their known bactericidal functional impairments (Repine et al., 1980; Gallacher et al., 1995), diabetic neutrophils still contribute to a degree in infection control in these wounds (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU count data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Despite their known bactericidal functional impairments, diabetic neutrophils still contribute to a degree in infection control in diabetic wounds.
source: Neutrophil-depletion also resulted in ~2 log-order more bacteria in diabetic wounds, indicating that despite their known bactericidal functional impairments (Repine et al., 1980; Gallacher et al., 1995), diabetic neutrophils still contribute to a degree in infection control in these wounds (Figure 4j).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that neutrophil-depletion resulted in more bacteria in diabetic wounds.

claim: Neutrophil-depletion abrogated CCL3's beneficial effects in boosting antimicrobial defenses against P. aeruginosa in diabetic wounds.
source: Importantly, neutrophil-depletion abrogated CCL3's beneficial effects in boosting antimicrobial defenses against P. aeruginosa in diabetic wounds (Figure 4j)
evidence: The claim is supported by CFU count data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: CCL3-induced enhanced infection control in diabetic wound is dependent on its ability to enhance neutrophil response in diabetic wound.
source: Importantly, neutrophil-depletion abrogated CCL3's beneficial effects in boosting antimicrobial defenses against P. aeruginosa in diabetic wounds (Figure 4j), indicating that CCL3-induced enhanced infection control in diabetic wound is dependent on its ability to enhance neutrophil response in diabetic wound.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that neutrophil-depletion abrogated CCL3's beneficial effects.

claim: Persistent non-resolving inflammation, as manifested by increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines and neutrophils, is considered a major contributor to healing impairment in diabetic foot ulcers.
source: Afterall, persistent non-resolving inflammation, (as manifested by increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines and neutrophils), is considered a major contributor to healing impairment in diabetic foot ulcers (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wetzler et al., 2000; Bjarnsholt et al., 2008).

claim: IL-1β and TNF-α pro-inflammatory cytokines are found to be elevated in chronic diabetic foot ulcers.
source: We assessed the long-term impact of CCL3 treatment on IL-1β and TNF-α pro-inflammatory cytokines that are found to be elevated in chronic diabetic foot ulcers (Mirza et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2016; Jeffcoate et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mirza et al., 2013; Yan et al., 2016; Jeffcoate et al., 2005).

claim: IL-1β and TNF-α continued to rise in the mock-treated db/db wounds as the diabetic wounds aged.
source: Data indicated that while IL-1β and TNF-α continued to rise in the mock-treated db/db wounds as the diabetic wounds aged, in the CCL3-treated diabetic wounds, these pro-inflammatory cytokines were significantly higher during the acute phase of healing early after injury but declined substantially in old wounds, particularly at day 10 (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5a–b.

claim: In the CCL3-treated diabetic wounds, IL-1β and TNF-α were significantly higher during the acute phase of healing early after injury but declined substantially in old wounds, particularly at day 10.
source: Data indicated that while IL-1β and TNF-α continued to rise in the mock-treated db/db wounds as the diabetic wounds aged, in the CCL3-treated diabetic wounds, these pro-inflammatory cytokines were significantly higher during the acute phase of healing early after injury but declined substantially in old wounds, particularly at day 10 (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5a–b.

claim: Neutrophil wound contents were highly elevated during the acute phase of healing early after injury in the CCL3-treated diabetic wounds but declined significantly as the wounds aged.
source: In line with these data, neutrophil wound contents (assessed by histological analysis using neutrophil marker Ly6G staining Pizza et al., 2005) were also highly elevated during the acute phase of healing early after injury in the CCL3-treated diabetic wounds but declined significantly as the wounds aged, as compared with the mock-treated diabetic wounds (Figure 5c–d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 5c–d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCL3 treatment significantly stimulated healing in infected diabetic wounds.
source: Encouragingly, CCL3 treatment also significantly stimulated healing in infected diabetic wounds, as assessed by wound area measurement (Figure 6a–b)
evidence: The claim is supported by wound area measurement data shown in Figure 6a–b.

claim: Mock-treated diabetic wounds became exacerbated as the result of P. aeruginosa infection.
source: Encouragingly, CCL3 treatment also significantly stimulated healing in infected diabetic wounds, as assessed by wound area measurement (Figure 6a–b), while mock-treated diabetic wounds became exacerbated as the result of P. aeruginosa infection as we have previously shown (Goldufsky et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by wound area measurement data shown in Figure 6a–b and a citation to a previous report (Goldufsky et al., 2015).

claim: CCL3-treated infected diabetic wounds were completely re-epithelized and exhibited epidermal thickening.
source: Corroborating these results, CCL3-treated infected diabetic wounds were completely re-epithelized and exhibited epidermal thickening as assessed by H&E histological analysis, while mock-treated infected diabetic wounds became exacerbated (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E histological analysis data shown in Figure 6c–d.

claim: Mock-treated infected diabetic wounds became exacerbated as assessed by H&E histological analysis.
source: Corroborating these results, CCL3-treated infected diabetic wounds were completely re-epithelized and exhibited epidermal thickening as assessed by H&E histological analysis, while mock-treated infected diabetic wounds became exacerbated (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E histological analysis data shown in Figure 6c–d.

claim: Fibroblasts and myofibroblasts are key players in extracellular matrix production and granulation tissue maturation during the proliferation and the remodeling phases of wound healing.
source: Fibroblasts and myofibroblasts are key players in extracellular matrix production and granulation tissue maturation during the proliferation and the remodeling phases of wound healing (Wilgus et al., 2008; Skalli et al., 1989; Cheng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wilgus et al., 2008; Skalli et al., 1989; Cheng et al., 2016).

claim: Persistent inflammatory environment in diabetic wounds adversely impacts the functions of fibroblast and myofibroblast, culminating in reduced collagen and elastin extracellular matrix deposition and impaired healing in diabetic chronic wounds.
source: However, persistent inflammatory environment in diabetic wounds adversely impacts the functions of fibroblast and myofibroblast, culminating in reduced collagen and elastin extracellular matrix deposition and impaired healing in diabetic chronic wounds (Diegelmann and Evans, 2004; Yue et al., 1986; Augustine et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Diegelmann and Evans, 2004; Yue et al., 1986; Augustine et al., 2014).

claim: P. aeruginosa infection further exacerbates inflammation and reduces collagen deposition in diabetic wounds.
source: P. aeruginosa infection further exacerbates inflammation and reduces collagen deposition in diabetic wounds (Goldufsky et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Goldufsky et al., 2015).

claim: CCL3-treated wounds showed significant increases in fibroblast, myofibroblast, collagen, and elastin healing markers.
source: CCL3-treated wounds showed significant increases in all these healing markers (Figure 6e–f and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 6e–f and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diabetic wounds are not destined to develop persistent non-resolving inflammation, provided that the dynamics of neutrophil trafficking is restored in these wounds early after injury.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that diabetic wounds are not destined to develop persistent non-resolving inflammation, provided that the dynamics of neutrophil trafficking is restored in these wounds early after injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that CCL3 treatment, which restores neutrophil trafficking, does not lead to persistent non-resolving inflammation.

claim: Exposure to glucose in diabetic range results in impaired chemotaxis signaling through the formyl peptide receptor (FPR) in neutrophils.
source: Here, we report that exposure to glucose in diabetic range results in impaired chemotaxis signaling through the formyl peptide receptor (FPR) in neutrophils, culminating in reduced chemotaxis and delayed neutrophil trafficking in the wound of Leprdb (db/db) type two diabetic mice, rendering diabetic wound vulnerable to infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing that exposure to high glucose impairs FPR signaling.

claim: Impaired FPR signaling culminates in reduced chemotaxis and delayed neutrophil trafficking in the wound of Leprdb (db/db) type two diabetic mice.
source: Here, we report that exposure to glucose in diabetic range results in impaired chemotaxis signaling through the formyl peptide receptor (FPR) in neutrophils, culminating in reduced chemotaxis and delayed neutrophil trafficking in the wound of Leprdb (db/db) type two diabetic mice, rendering diabetic wound vulnerable to infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing delayed neutrophil trafficking in diabetic wounds.

claim: Delayed neutrophil trafficking renders diabetic wound vulnerable to infection.
source: Here, we report that exposure to glucose in diabetic range results in impaired chemotaxis signaling through the formyl peptide receptor (FPR) in neutrophils, culminating in reduced chemotaxis and delayed neutrophil trafficking in the wound of Leprdb (db/db) type two diabetic mice, rendering diabetic wound vulnerable to infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing delayed neutrophil trafficking and increased bacterial burden in diabetic wounds.

claim: At least some auxiliary receptors remain functional under diabetic conditions.
source: We further show that at least some auxiliary receptors remain functional under diabetic conditions and their engagement by the pro-inflammatory cytokine CCL3, overrides the requirement for FPR signaling and substantially improves infection control by jumpstarting the neutrophil trafficking toward infection, and stimulates healing in diabetic wound.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that CCR1 and CXCR2 remain functional under diabetic conditions.

claim: Engagement of auxiliary receptors by CCL3 overrides the requirement for FPR signaling and substantially improves infection control by jumpstarting the neutrophil trafficking toward infection.
source: We further show that at least some auxiliary receptors remain functional under diabetic conditions and their engagement by the pro-inflammatory cytokine CCL3, overrides the requirement for FPR signaling and substantially improves infection control by jumpstarting the neutrophil trafficking toward infection, and stimulates healing in diabetic wound.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that CCL3 treatment enhances neutrophil trafficking and infection control in diabetic wounds.

claim: CCL3 stimulates healing in diabetic wound.
source: We further show that at least some auxiliary receptors remain functional under diabetic conditions and their engagement by the pro-inflammatory cytokine CCL3, overrides the requirement for FPR signaling and substantially improves infection control by jumpstarting the neutrophil trafficking toward infection, and stimulates healing in diabetic wound.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that CCL3 treatment stimulates healing in diabetic wounds.

claim: CCL3 may have therapeutic potential for the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers if it is applied topically after the surgical debridement process.
source: We posit that CCL3 may have therapeutic potential for the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers if it is applied topically after the surgical debridement process which is intended to reset chronic ulcers into acute fresh wounds.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: Early after injury, the diabetic wound exhibits a paradoxical and damaging decrease in essential neutrophil trafficking.
source: Here, we demonstrate that early after injury, the diabetic wound exhibits a paradoxical and damaging decrease in essential neutrophil trafficking, which in turn renders diabetic wounds vulnerable to infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing reduced neutrophil influx in diabetic wounds early after injury.

claim: Impaired signaling through FPR is an important culprit responsible for the delay in the neutrophil response to injury and infection in diabetic wounds.
source: Our data point to impaired signaling through FPR (resulting from exposure to high glucose levels), as an important culprit responsible for the delay in the neutrophil response to injury and infection in diabetic wounds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that exposure to high glucose impairs FPR signaling and that this correlates with delayed neutrophil response.

claim: Even a short-term rise in serum glucose levels could potentially make non-diabetic people transiently immunocompromised and susceptible to infection.
source: It is worth noting that 1 hr exposure to high glucose levels dramatically impaired chemotaxis signaling through the FPR in neutrophils, suggesting that even a short-term rise in serum glucose levels could potentially make non-diabetic people transiently immunocompromised and susceptible to infection.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the observation that 1 hr exposure to high glucose impairs FPR signaling.

claim: Hyperglycemia during the perioperative and postoperative periods are significant risk factors for surgical site infection (SSI).
source: In line with this notion, hyperglycemia during the perioperative and postoperative periods are found to be significant risk factors for surgical site infection (SSI) (Ambiru et al., 2008; Sadoskas et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ambiru et al., 2008; Sadoskas et al., 2016).

claim: Glycemic control during the perioperative period has been shown to significantly reduce SSI rates both in human and in animals.
source: while glycemic control during the perioperative period has been shown to significantly reduce SSI rates both in human and in animals (Kroin et al., 2015; Sadoskas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kroin et al., 2015; Sadoskas et al., 2016).

claim: Neutrophils play a pivotal role in the resolution phase of inflammation through the production and release of anti-inflammatory and inflammation resolving proteins and bioactive lipids, such as Annexin A1, lipoxins, and protectin D1.
source: This finding is consistent with reports highlighting the pivotal role of neutrophils also in the resolution phase of inflammation (through the production and release of anti-inflammatory and inflammation resolving proteins and bioactive lipids, such as Annexin A1, lipoxins, and protectin D1), to ensure that the inflammatory responses cease safely without compromising tissue's defenses against invading pathogens, which they accomplish directly (Jones et al., 2016; Sugimoto et al., 2016; Serhan et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jones et al., 2016; Sugimoto et al., 2016; Serhan et al., 2008).

claim: Defective signaling through FPR2 in neutrophils may be a contributing factor to the sustained non-resolving inflammatory environment in chronic diabetic ulcers.
source: Given that FPR2 has been implicated in the resolution of inflammation in response to Annexin A1, lipoxin A4, and resolving D1 inflammation pro-resolving agonists (Ye et al., 2009; Jeong and Bae, 2020; Bena et al., 2012; Yazid et al., 2012; Serhan and Savill, 2005), these data suggest that defective signaling through FPR2 in neutrophils may also be a contributing factor to the sustained non-resolving inflammatory environment in chronic diabetic ulcers.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the observation that high glucose reduces FPR2 expression and the known role of FPR2 in inflammation resolution.

claim: The purpose of surgical debridement is to convert a chronic non-healing wound environment into an acute healing environment through the removal of necrotic and infected tissue, and the senescent and non-responsive cells.
source: The purpose of surgical debridement, which is performed as a standard-of-care weekly or biweekly in the clinics, is to convert a chronic non-healing wound environment into an acute healing environment through the removal of necrotic and infected tissue, and the senescent and non-responsive cells (Golinko et al., 2008; Lebrun et al., 2010; Cardinal et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Golinko et al., 2008; Lebrun et al., 2010; Cardinal et al., 2009).
